source_text: Τί οὖν; ἐν τῇ κατηγορίᾳ τοῦ κακοῦ τὸν λόγον στήσομεν; Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ὥσπερ ἥμισύ τί ἐστι τῆς ἰατρείας. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ δεῖξαι τῷ κάμνοντι τῆς νόσου τὸ μέγε θος, ὥστε ἀξίαν ἐμποιῆσαι αὐτῷ τοῦ κακοῦ τὴν φροντίδα, οὐκ ἄχρηστον· τὸ δὲ ἄχρι τούτου καταλιπεῖν, μὴ πρὸς τὴν ὑγίειαν χειραγωγήσαντα, οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστιν ἢ ἔκδοτον ἀφεῖναι τῇ ἀῤῥωστίᾳ τὸν κάμνοντα. Τί οὖν; πῶς ἂν μὴ πάθοιμεν ἐξ ἀρχῆς τὴν νόσον, ἢ ὑπαχθέντες ἐκφύγοιμεν; Εἰ πρῶτον μὲν μηδὲν μέγα, μηδὲ ὑπερφυὲς τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων κρίνοιμεν· μὴ εὐπορίαν τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις· μὴ δόξαν τὴν ἀπανθοῦσαν· μὴ σώματος εὐεξίαν. Οὐ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς παρερχομένοις ὁριζόμεθα εἶναι τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ αἰωνίων ἀγαθῶν καὶ ἀληθινῶν μετ ουσίαν κεκλήμεθα. Ὥστε ὁ πλουτῶν οὔπω ζηλωτός ἐστι διὰ τὸν πλοῦτον· οὐχ ὁ δυνάστης διὰ τὸν ὄγκον τοῦ ἀξιώματος, οὐχ ὁ ἰσχυρὸς διὰ τὴν ῥώμην τοῦ σώματος, οὐχ ὁ σοφὸς διὰ τὴν τοῦ λόγου περιου σίαν. Ὄργανα γάρ ἐστι ταῦτα τῆς ἀρετῆς τοῖς κα λῶς κεχρημένοις, οὐκ αὐτὰ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχοντα τὸ μα κάριον. Ὁ μὲν οὖν κακῶς αὐτοῖς κεχρημένος, ἐλεει νὸς, ὡς ὁ τῷ ξίφει, ὃ ἔλαβε πρὸς τὴν τῶν πολεμίων ἄμυναν, τούτῳ ἑκουσίως ἑαυτὸν κατατιτρώσκων· εἰ δὲ καλῶς καὶ κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον τὰ παρόντα με ταχειρίζεται, καὶ οἰκονόμος ἐστὶ τῶν παρὰ Θεοῦ, οὐχὶ δὲ πρὸς ἰδίαν ἀπόλαυσιν θησαυρίζει, ἐπαινεῖσθαι καὶ ἀγαπᾶσθαι δίκαιός ἐστι διὰ τὸ φιλάδελφον καὶ κοινωνικὸν τοῦ τρόπου. Πάλιν φρονήσει τις διαφέ ρει, καὶ λόγῳ Θεοῦ τετίμηται, καὶ ἐξηγητής ἐστιν ἱερῶν λογίων· μὴ φθονήσῃς τῷ τοιούτῳ, μηδὲ βουληθῇς ποτε σιωπῆσαι τὸν τῶν ἱερῶν ὑποφήτην, εἰ τῇ τοῦ Πνεύματος χάριτι ἀποδοχή τις καὶ ἔπαινος ἐκ τῶν ἀκουόντων ἀκολουθεῖ. Σὸν γάρ ἐστι τὸ ἀγα θὸν, καί σοι ἐπέμφθη διὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τῆς διδασκα λίας τὸ δῶρον, ἐὰν ὑποδέξασθαι θέλῃς. Εἶτα, πηγὴν μὲν βρύουσαν οὐδεὶς ἐμφράσσει· καὶ ἡλίου λάμποντος οὐδεὶς τὰς ὄψεις ἐπικαλύπτει, οὐδὲ βασκαίνει ἐκείνοις, ἀλλ' ἑαυτῷ συνεύχεται τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν· λόγου δὲ πνευματικοῦ ἐν Ἐκκλησίᾳ βρύοντος, καὶ καρδίας εὐσεβοῦς ἐκ τῶν χαρισμάτων τοῦ Πνεύματος πηγαζούσης, οὐχ ὑπέχεις τὰς ἀκοὰς μετ' εὐφροσύνης; οὐκ εὐχαρίστως ὑποδέχῃ τὴν ὠφέλειαν; Ἀλλὰ δάκνει σε ὁ κρότος τῶν ἀκουόντων, καὶ ἐβουλήθης ἂν μήτε τὸν ὠφελούμενον εἶναι, μήτε τὸν ἐπαινοῦντα. Τίνα ταῦτα ἀπολογίαν ἕξει ἐπὶ τοῦ κριτοῦ τῶν καρδιῶν ἡμῶν; Φύσει μὲν οὖν εἶναι καλὸν ἡγεῖσθαι χρὴ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀγαθόν· τὸν δὲ ὑπερανθοῦντα τῷ πλούτῳ, καὶ δυναστείᾳ μέγα φρονοῦντα, καὶ εὐεξίᾳ σώματος, καὶ καλῶς μὲν κεχρημένον οἷς ἔχει, ἀγαπᾷν καὶ περιέπειν, ὡς κοινὰ τὰ τοῦ βίου ὄργανα κεκτημένον, εἴπερ δὴ ταῦτα κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον μεταχειρίζοιτο· ὡς τῇ μὲν τῶν χρημάτων χορηγίᾳ ἄφθονος εἶναι τοῖς δεομένοις, τῷ σώματι δὲ ὑπηρεσίαν παρέχειν τοῖς ἀσθενοῦσι· πᾶσαν δὲ τὴν λοιπὴν περιουσίαν οὐ μᾶλλον ἑαυτοῦ νομίζειν, ἢ καὶ οὑτινοσοῦν τῶν ἐπιδεομένων· τὸν δὲ μὴ οὕτω πρὸς ταῦτα διακείμενον ἄθλιον τίθεσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ ἐπίφθονον, εἰ μείζονας ἔχει πρὸς τὸ κακὸς εἶναι τὰς ἀφορμάς.
thought_title: The remedy: judge goods as instruments, not as the good itself
orientation: Basil has just finished describing the destructiveness of envy and now turns to the cure, beginning with how to regard worldly goods.
pass_a_gloss: What then? Shall we stop the discourse at the accusation of the evil? But this is, as it were, half of the healing. For to show the sick person the magnitude of the disease, so as to produce in him a worthy concern for the evil, is not useless; but to leave off at this point, not having led him by the hand toward health, is nothing other than to send the sick person away abandoned to the sickness. What then? How might we not suffer the disease from the beginning, or having been brought under it, escape it? If first we judge nothing great, nothing supernatural among human things; not abundance among men; not glory that fades; not good condition of body. For we are not defined to be in the good among passing things, but we have been called to a share of eternal and true goods. So the rich man is not yet enviable because of wealth; not the ruler because of the bulk of his dignity, not the strong man because of the strength of his body, not the wise man because of the abundance of speech. For these are instruments of virtue for those who use them well, not things having in themselves the blessed. The one then who uses them badly is pitiable, as the one who with the sword, which he received for defense against enemies, with this willingly wounds himself; but if he handles present things well and according to right reason, and is a steward of the things from God, and does not treasure them up for private enjoyment, he is justly praised and loved because of the brother-loving and sharing character of his manner. Again, someone excels in prudence, and has been honored with the word of God, and is an interpreter of sacred oracles; do not envy such a one, nor ever wish the interpreter of sacred things to be silent, if by the grace of the Spirit some acceptance and praise from the hearers follows. For the good is yours, and to you was sent through the brother the gift of teaching, if you are willing to receive it. Then, no one blocks up a gushing spring; and when the sun shines no one covers his eyes, nor envies those things, but prays with himself for the enjoyment; but when spiritual speech gushes in the Church, and a pious heart springs from the gifts of the Spirit, do you not hold out your ears with gladness? Do you not receive the benefit with thanksgiving? But the applause of the hearers bites you, and you would have wished neither the one being benefited to exist, nor the one praising. What defense will these things have before the judge of our hearts? By nature then one must consider the good of the soul to be beautiful; but the one overflowing with wealth, and thinking great things because of power, and good condition of body, and using well what he has, to love and to cherish, as one possessing the instruments of life as common, if indeed he handles these according to right reason; so as by the supply of money to be ungrudging to those in need, and with the body to provide service to the weak; and to consider all the remaining abundance not more his own than also any one of those in need; but the one not so disposed toward these things to regard as wretched rather than enviable, if he has greater starting points for being bad.

choices.why: Basil frames the homily as medical treatment; 'healing' keeps the therapeutic metaphor consistent with 'sick person' and 'sickness' in the same sentence.
ἔκδοτος means handed over or given up; 'abandoned' captures the sense of leaving the sick person without further care, matching Basil's medical frame.
The word means beyond nature; Basil is saying nothing human should be judged as beyond the ordinary, so 'supernatural' preserves the literal sense of exceeding nature.
The verb means to lose bloom or flower; 'fading' keeps the botanical image of glory that withers, which Basil contrasts with eternal goods.
ὄγκος means mass or bulk; Basil uses it to suggest the inflated weight of high office, so 'bulk' preserves the physical metaphor rather than smoothing it over.
The term means one who speaks forth sacred things; 'interpreter' matches the preceding 'interpreter of sacred oracles' and keeps the priestly-prophetic role Basil describes.
The compound suggests praying along with or for oneself; Basil means the person wishes for his own enjoyment, so 'prays with himself' keeps the reflexive force.
The word means clapping or applause; Basil is describing the envious person's irritation at the hearers' approval, so 'applause' is the precise social sense.
The verb means to bloom beyond or abound; 'overflowing' keeps the image of excess that Basil uses to describe the rich man's abundance.
The word means resources or bases of operation; Basil says the bad rich man has greater starting points for being bad, so 'starting points' preserves the military metaphor of a base for action.

pass_b_english: What then? Shall we stop the discourse at the accusation of the evil? But this is only half the healing. To show the sick person the magnitude of his disease, so as to make him take the evil seriously, is not useless. But to leave him there, without leading him by the hand toward health, is nothing other than to send the sick person away abandoned to his sickness. What then? How might we avoid suffering the disease from the beginning, or escape it once we have been caught? First, if we judge nothing human to be great or supernatural: not the wealth that exists among people, not the glory that blooms and fades, not the body's vigor. For we are not called to define the good in things that pass away, but to share in eternal and true goods. So the rich man is not yet enviable because of his wealth; nor the ruler because of the bulk of his dignity; nor the strong man because of his bodily power; nor the wise man because of his abundance of speech. For these are instruments of virtue for those who use them well; they do not in themselves possess blessedness. The one who uses them badly is pitiable, like a man who takes a sword he received for defense against enemies and willingly wounds himself with it. But if a man handles present things well and according to right reason, and is a steward of what comes from God, not treasuring them up for his own enjoyment, he is rightly praised and loved because of his brother-loving and sharing character. Again, someone excels in wisdom, and has been honored with the word of God, and is an interpreter of sacred oracles. Do not envy such a person, and do not ever wish the interpreter of sacred things to fall silent, if by the grace of the Spirit some acceptance and praise from the hearers follows him. For the good is yours, and the gift of teaching was sent to you through your brother, if you are willing to receive it. No one blocks up a gushing spring; no one covers his eyes when the sun shines, nor envies those things, but prays to share in their enjoyment. But when spiritual speech gushes in the Church, and a devout heart springs from the gifts of the Spirit, do you not hold out your ears with gladness? Do you not receive the benefit with gratitude? Instead, the applause of the hearers bites you, and you would wish that neither the one being helped nor the one praising existed. What defense will these things have before the judge of our hearts? By nature, then, one must consider the good of the soul to be beautiful. And the one overflowing with wealth, and thinking great things because of his power, and his body's vigor, and using well what he has—love him and cherish him, as one who possesses the common instruments of life, if indeed he handles these things according to right reason: so that by the supply of his money he is ungrudging to those in need, and with his body he provides service to the weak; and he considers all the rest of his abundance no more his own than that of anyone in need. But the one who is not so disposed toward these things, consider him wretched rather than enviable, since he has greater starting points for being bad.

problems.why: συνεὔχεται means 'prays along with, joins in prayer' or 'prays for himself to share in'; 'prays with himself' is awkward and unclear.
problems.fix: prays to share in their enjoyment

problems.why: ἀπανθοῦσαν means 'blooming, flourishing' (from ἄνθος, flower), not 'fades'; it's transient glory that blooms then withers.
problems.fix: not the glory that blooms [and fades]
problems.ruling: ἀπανθοῦσαν means 'blooming/flourishing' not 'fades'; opposite sense, misleading reader about transient glory.

problems.quote: not his own rather than any one of those in need
problems.source_quote: οὐ μᾶλλον ἑαυτοῦ νομίζειν, ἢ καὶ οὑτινοσοῦν τῶν ἐπιδεομένων
problems.why: The Greek says he should consider abundance 'no more his own than that of anyone in need'; English reverses to 'not his own rather than', changing meaning.
problems.fix: no more his own than that of anyone in need
problems.ruling: οὐ μᾶλλον...ἢ means 'no more his own than anyone in need's'; English 'not his own rather than' reverses meaning.

fixed: συνεὔχεται means 'prays along with' or 'prays to share in'; 'prays with himself' misstates the source.
ἀπανθοῦσαν means 'blooming' (from ἄνθος, flower), not 'fades'; the glory blooms then withers.
οὐ μᾶλλον ἑαυτοῦ νομίζειν, ἢ καὶ οὑτινοσοῦν means 'no more his own than that of anyone'; the English reversed the comparison.

last_rejected.quote: not the glory that blooms and fades
last_rejected.why: ἀπανθόω means 'blooming' (like flowers), not 'blooms and fades'; adds fading not in source.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπανθόω means 'to bloom, then fade/wither' (flowers losing bloom); 'blooms and fades' captures this standard meaning accurately.

last_rejected.why: ὑπερφυὲς means 'extraordinary' or 'outstanding', not 'supernatural' which implies beyond nature/divine.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπερφυὲς literally means 'beyond nature'; 'supernatural' is within its semantic range and fits the context.

last_rejected.why: ὄγκος here means 'pomp' or 'grandeur', not physical 'bulk'; this misreads the metaphor.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Bulk of his dignity' is a literal rendering of ὄγκον τοῦ ἀξιώματος; 'bulk' can mean grandeur figuratively. Not a major error.

last_rejected.why: περιουσία means 'abundance/wealth', but λόγος here is 'reason' or 'eloquence', not mere 'speech'; 'abundance of reason' or 'eloquence' better.
last_rejected.ruling: λόγος can mean 'speech'; 'abundance of speech' is within normal range. Preference for 'reason' or 'eloquence' is not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: prays to share in their enjoyment
last_rejected.why: συνεύχεται means 'prays for' not 'prays to share in'; the reflexive ἑαυτῷ shows he prays for himself to have enjoyment.
last_rejected.fix: prays for himself to enjoy them
last_rejected.ruling: ἑαυτῷ συνεύχεται τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν: 'prays to share in their enjoyment' captures the sense adequately; reflexive nuance is minor.

last_rejected.quote: thinking great things because of his power
last_rejected.why: δυναστεία is 'power/authority' but μέγα φρονεῖν is 'to be proud/haughty', not 'thinking great things'; 'proud of his power'.
last_rejected.ruling: μέγα φρονεῖν literally means 'think great things'; 'thinking great things because of his power' is within normal range. Minor preference.

last_rejected.why: ἄφθονος means 'generous/bountiful', not 'ungrudging' which suggests reluctance; the sense is open-handed giving.
last_rejected.ruling: ἄφθονος means 'without envy/grudging'; 'ungrudging' is within its semantic range. Preference for 'generous' is not a major error.

last_rejected.why: ἀφορμαί are 'means/opportunities', not 'starting points'; and κακὸς εἶναι is 'to be evil/wicked', weakend to 'being bad'.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀφορμαί can mean 'starting points'; 'being bad' for κακὸς εἶναι is within normal range. Preference for 'opportunities/evil' is minor.
